title: Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an anesthetic strategy that prevents a clinically meaningful share of postoperative brain dysfunction by targeting a demonstrated causal pathway. It would identify a harmful biological process that anesthetic management can substantially modify, then adjust drugs, dosing or other aspects of anesthesia to interrupt that process while maintaining unconsciousness and physiological stability. The defining advance would be a demonstrated connection between mechanism, intervention and improved patient outcomes.

Conceptual distinction: postoperative delirium and persistent cognitive decline are separate outcomes and require separate assessment. Delirium concerns an acute disturbance of attention and mental function; longer-term decline concerns cognitive changes that persist beyond the immediate recovery period. Preventing one would not establish prevention of the other. The concept also allows for multiple contributing causes: anesthesia would need to influence an actionable pathway without being assumed to explain every postoperative cognitive problem.

A central scientific distinction is the difference between a risk marker and a treatment target. An EEG pattern associated with delirium could reflect vulnerability, drug exposure or another underlying process. That association alone would not show that changing the pattern prevents delirium. A successful mechanism-guided intervention would need evidence that modifying its target changes the relevant clinical outcome.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: reliably preventing substantial postoperative delirium or persistent cognitive decline through anesthetic management would add a major protective capability to surgical care. If both outcomes were reduced, the advance would span immediate postoperative brain function and longer-term cognitive recovery. Its importance would depend on the size and durability of benefit, the patients and operations covered, and the burdens or risks introduced by treatment.

Reduced delirium could improve immediate recovery, but trials would need to measure whether patients also experience better function, independence or quality of life. Downstream benefits such as reduced care needs would remain conditional on those results. An improvement in an EEG measure or cognitive test score would not, by itself, establish all of these practical benefits.

The impact has important boundaries. Prevention of dementia would require separate evidence, as would protection against cognitive problems arising from surgery, critical illness or other causes beyond the intervention's demonstrated pathway. Even an effective anesthesia-centered intervention would not imply universal prevention or elimination of overall perioperative neurological risk. Calling the capability revolutionary is a conditional judgment about what successful demonstration would enable, rather than a claim that a source has endorsed that judgment or that the capability already exists.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability, as framed by this proposal, is to identify and effectively modify a causal pathway connecting anesthetic management to postoperative brain dysfunction. This requires distinguishing effects of anesthetic exposure from patient vulnerability, the operation, illness and other perioperative influences. The supplied review considers this framing scientifically coherent, but the available evidence package does not establish the complete state of the field at the intended assessment date.

A concrete scientific barrier is determining whether a measurable signal lies on a harmful causal pathway or merely accompanies it. EEG suppression illustrates the problem: changing a monitored signal may alter drug exposure without changing the biological process responsible for delirium. Conversely, failure of one strategy would not establish that every anesthesia-modifiable mechanism is ineffective. Mechanistic measurements and randomized intervention evidence would need to be interpreted together.

Engineering and clinical barriers include selecting an actionable target, measuring it reliably enough to guide treatment, and delivering an intervention within a safe anesthetic range. Reducing exposure or changing drugs must preserve adequate unconsciousness and physiological stability. Patient differences and procedural demands may change both the useful treatment window and the mechanism's relevance, so a strategy effective in one surgical population may need further validation elsewhere.

Outcome measurement is another barrier. Acute delirium and persistent cognitive decline need distinct definitions, assessment schedules and analyses. A convincing program would also need to distinguish clinically meaningful benefit from changes limited to a surrogate measure, and determine whether any early advantage persists. These are proposed research requirements; the supplied material does not document an established protocol that resolves them.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies the ENGAGES-Canada randomized clinical trial, attributed to André Deschamps, Avidan Ben Abdallah, Eric Jacobsohn and colleagues, as published online in JAMA on 10 June 2024, with DOI 10.1001/jama.2024.8144. It reports that EEG-guided anesthesia intended to minimize suppression did not reduce postoperative delirium compared with usual care in older adults undergoing cardiac surgery. However, the source index contains no captured abstract, full text or other retained artifact. The supplied review therefore could not independently verify the bibliographic identity, population, treatment comparison or findings. This is a reported dated result with an explicit verification limitation, rather than an independently confirmed result within this evidence package.

If the supplied account of ENGAGES-Canada is accurate, its conclusion concerns that EEG-guided strategy, comparator and cardiac-surgery population. It would caution against assuming that minimizing EEG suppression necessarily prevents delirium. It would not establish that all EEG-guided approaches fail, that anesthesia has no causal contribution, or that persistent cognitive decline cannot be prevented. The supplied materials provide no verifiable effect estimates, event counts or confidence intervals, so the magnitude and precision of the reported finding remain unspecified here.

The research also reports that a multidisciplinary prevention program reduced delirium after some elective procedures. No identifiable supporting source or source text accompanies that assertion, so its intervention components, population, date, effect size and findings remain unverified. Even if confirmed, benefit from a multidisciplinary program would not by itself identify an anesthesia-specific causal mechanism or establish prevention of long-term cognitive decline.

The research describes a selective assessment including selected evidence through 1 November 2026, rather than a systematic review. The validated review found no freshness record and no retained artifact for the listed 2024 publication. Consequently, these inputs cannot determine whether later evidence changed the field or establish that the proposed capability remained unachieved on that date. Missing artifacts limit verification; they do not demonstrate that a reported result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: establish a credible causal chain from a specified anesthetic intervention, through a measurable biological pathway, to reduced postoperative brain dysfunction. Evidence should address plausible competing explanations and show why the chosen target is actionable. Merely predicting delirium or changing an EEG pattern would not complete this demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Anesthetic intervention causally reduces postoperative brain dysfunction through measurable pathway

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical validation: independent, multicenter randomized trials should show a clinically meaningful reduction in delirium across clearly defined operations and patient risk groups. Where prevention of persistent cognitive decline is claimed, trials should assess it separately using prespecified measures, follow-up periods and analyses. The terms 'substantial' benefit and 'persistent' decline require operational definitions before testing; no numerical threshold or duration is established by the supplied evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent multicenter randomized trials demonstrate clinically meaningful delirium reduction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical validation: trials should assess functional recovery and other patient-important outcomes alongside awareness, physiological instability and other harms relevant to the intervention. Reproducibility would require sufficiently described treatment protocols, target measurements, adherence and outcome assessment for independent teams to repeat the work. Evidence of benefit should include uncertainty estimates and the practical resources required to deliver treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible evaluations quantify patient benefits, harms and treatment resource requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope boundary: successful trials would establish benefit within their demonstrated populations, procedures and treatment conditions. Broader claims would require additional evidence, including examination of groups with different vulnerabilities or perioperative demands. Finite testing can demonstrate substantial breadth and reproducibility, but cannot establish literal universality. Dementia prevention would remain a separate claim requiring an appropriate study design and follow-up.
completion_criteria.label: Benefit claims match demonstrated populations, procedures and treatment conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ANS-01, 'A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness,' could supply mechanistic tools for understanding anesthetic effects, while ANS-02, 'A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia,' could help assess whether a protective intervention preserves adequate unconsciousness. Their targets remain distinct: explaining or monitoring conscious experience does not establish prevention of postoperative delirium or persistent cognitive decline.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-04, 'Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control,' addresses physiological functions that may matter when designing a safe brain-protection strategy. ANS-06, 'Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia,' concerns ending anesthetic effects. Preserved physiological control or faster emergence could overlap with recovery goals, but neither alone demonstrates protection against postoperative brain dysfunction.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-03, 'A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block,' and ANS-07, 'Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain,' could change perioperative pain treatment and drug exposure. Any cognitive benefit from those changes would need direct testing. ANS-09, 'Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain,' shares the ambition of preventing a lasting postoperative complication through a causal mechanism, but addresses a different outcome and would require its own evidence.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-05, 'A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery,' could eventually help deliver a proven brain-protective protocol, although accessibility and resilience do not establish its efficacy. ANS-08, 'Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway,' concerns rescue from a different perioperative threat. Neither concept substitutes for demonstrating the specific causal and clinical effects proposed in ANS-10.

The concept also overlaps with perioperative medicine, geriatrics, neuroscience and cardiac surgery. Its anesthesia-specific identity depends on demonstrating that anesthetic management substantially modifies the causal pathway. A successful general delirium-prevention program could be clinically valuable without satisfying that particular requirement.

unresolved_issues: The identity, methods and findings of the listed ENGAGES-Canada publication remain unverified within the supplied artifact-free evidence package.
The multidisciplinary prevention program is not identified or sourced, leaving its scope, date and reported benefit unresolved.
The supplied material does not identify a validated anesthesia-modifiable causal pathway or establish which intervention could successfully target it.
The clinical burden and multiple-cause characterization lack retained supporting source text in this evidence package.
No freshness record establishes whether subsequent evidence changed the field through 1 November 2026.
Trial designers would need to define clinically meaningful benefit, persistent cognitive decline, follow-up duration, safety boundaries and intended patient populations.
No review recommendation was rejected; unresolved evidence questions were retained as qualifications rather than converted into findings of falsity.

brief.title: Anesthesia that protects thinking after surgery
possible: People having surgery could receive anesthesia chosen to prevent delirium, an acute disturbance of attention and thinking, or lasting problems with memory and thought. Doctors would adjust treatment to interrupt a harmful biological process while keeping patients unconscious and physically stable.
why: Preventing delirium would improve immediate recovery after surgery. Preventing lasting cognitive decline would extend protection into longer-term recovery. An effective strategy would make protecting brain function a demonstrated part of anesthetic care.

sources.who: André Deschamps, Avidan Ben Abdallah, Eric Jacobsohn and colleagues
sources.showed: This randomized trial compared anesthesia guided by electrical brain activity with usual care in older adults undergoing heart surgery.
sources.cited_for: It tests whether adjusting anesthesia using brain activity can prevent delirium.
sources.not_established: It does not establish an anesthesia treatment that prevents delirium through a demonstrated biological pathway.

sources.showed: In a randomized study within the BALANCED trial, patients assigned lighter anesthesia had less delirium and better later cognitive screening results than those assigned deeper anesthesia.
sources.quote:
Among patients undergoing major surgery, targeting light anaesthesia reduced the risk of postoperative
delirium and cognitive impairment at 1 yr.
sources.cited_for: Changing anesthetic depth can affect delirium risk under the conditions tested.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish which biological pathway caused the benefit or whether patients gained better function or independence.

shown: Lisbeth Evered and colleagues found less delirium with lighter anesthesia in the BALANCED trial’s delirium study. Cognitive screening also favored lighter anesthesia a year later. This supports adjusting anesthesia, but does not identify the biological process responsible.

ENGAGES-Canada reported that guiding anesthesia to minimize suppression of electrical brain activity did not reduce delirium in older heart-surgery patients. Changing a brain signal therefore cannot simply be assumed to prevent delirium.
missing: A demonstrated causal pathway that anesthesia can safely modify to prevent postoperative problems with thinking.
Independent trials confirming meaningful delirium prevention, with lasting cognitive decline assessed separately.
Repeatable evidence of better everyday recovery, alongside treatment risks and the resources needed to deliver care.

milestones.label: A treatment interrupts a harmful pathway and protects thinking
milestones.explanation: An anesthetic intervention would have to change a measurable biological process and thereby reduce postoperative brain dysfunction. This would establish a treatment target rather than a signal that merely predicts risk.

milestones.label: Independent trials confirm meaningful delirium prevention
milestones.explanation: Independent randomized trials across hospitals would have to show meaningful delirium reduction in defined patient groups and operations. Separate testing of lasting cognitive decline would establish whether protection extends beyond delirium.

milestones.label: Repeatable studies establish patient benefits, harms and resource needs
milestones.explanation: Repeatable evaluations would have to measure everyday recovery, treatment harms and resource needs using clearly described protocols. This would establish whether the benefit translates into practical patient care.

milestones.label: Protection holds within clearly demonstrated treatment conditions
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to establish which patients, operations and treatment conditions benefit, with further testing for broader claims. This would define the protection’s reach; dementia prevention would require separate evidence.

uncertain: Which measurable biological process is a cause of harm that anesthesia can change, rather than a sign of patient vulnerability?
How large must a benefit be to matter clinically, and how long must cognitive changes last to count as persistent?
How do patient vulnerability and the demands of different operations change the safe treatment window?

page.title: Mechanism-guided prevention of perioperative neurocognitive disorders
page.definition: Anesthetic management prevents postoperative delirium, an acute disturbance of attention and awareness, or postoperative neurocognitive disorder, cognitive decline diagnosed from 30 days to 12 months after surgery, by interrupting a demonstrated causal pathway. The outcomes require separate evidence.

goal.need: ENGAGES-Canada randomized 1,140 adults aged at least 60 years undergoing cardiac surgery. About 18% developed delirium during postoperative days 1–5. Electroencephalography (EEG), which records brain electrical activity, guided an intervention that reduced EEG suppression without reducing delirium. Changing an anesthesia-associated signal therefore does not establish clinical prevention.

figures.caption: ENGAGES-Canada: target engagement and postoperative delirium
figures.note: Delirium was assessed during postoperative days 1–5. Denominators are participants assessed for the primary outcome. The delirium risk difference was 0.05 percentage points (95% CI −4.57 to 4.67).

completion.title: A randomized human experiment demonstrates causal prevention of a diagnosed postoperative disorder.
completion.criterion: For each outcome separately, a randomized human experiment shows that selective manipulation of an anesthesia-modifiable pathway reduces diagnosed disease versus a prespecified comparator at the registered protocol’s superiority threshold, while meeting its safety criteria. Target engagement and pathway-specific perturbation establish the causal link. Delirium uses a diagnostic endpoint; postoperative neurocognitive disorder requires cognitive concern, domain-specific objective decline and assessment of daily function from 30 days to 12 months.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external completion standard combining clinical prevention with demonstrated human causation was found.
completion.basis: Searches of ASA brain-health goals, ASER/POQI research priorities, the ESAIC guideline, FDA delirium-prevention guidance and ENGAGES/BALANCED protocols found no common completion test, minimum clinical benefit or human causal-validation threshold. This fallback combines the published prevention and mechanism goals. Consensus nomenclature supplies the outcome definitions; it does not establish anesthetic causation.

milestones.title: Pathway-specific inhibition reverses an experimental postanesthetic behavioural deficit.
milestones.criterion: Selective pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion prevents or reverses a measured postanesthetic behavioural deficit versus anesthetic-exposed controls. Zurek et al., published 3 November 2014, reversed object-recognition impairment after etomidate 8 mg/kg with the α5-containing GABA-A receptor inhibitor L-655,708, 0.5 mg/kg; Figure 3A used 6–11 mice per group. This supports an anesthetic-memory mechanism. It establishes neither an animal delirium phenotype nor persistent human neurocognitive disorder.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of the ASA preclinical-science report and ESAIC guideline found no shared preclinical efficacy gate. Experimental pathway rescue is used without inventing a numerical translational threshold.

milestones.title: EEG-guided anesthesia reduces anesthetic exposure and EEG suppression compared with usual care.
milestones.criterion: EEG-guided surgical patients receive less anesthetic and have less EEG suppression than usual-care patients. The ENGAGES pilot randomized 117 patients: median age-adjusted minimum alveolar concentration, an inhaled-anesthetic dose measure, was 0.78 versus 0.93, P<0.001; its Results section also reports reduced EEG suppression. This meets the programme’s target-engagement milestone for its delirium strategy, without establishing prevention of either clinical outcome.
milestones.set_by: National Institute on Aging, ENGAGES investigators and Westat; UH2-to-UH3 progression milestones, Table 1, reported in 2018. The criterion was written for EEG-guided delirium prevention.
milestones.threshold_quote: Establish treatment arm fidelity by assessing whether EEG-guided patients are administered less anesthetic and demonstrate reduced EEG suppression compared to standard care patients

milestones.title: An anesthetic intervention lowers a diagnosed neurocognitive endpoint at two-sided P<0.05.
milestones.criterion: A randomized comparison lowers a diagnosed endpoint at two-sided P<0.05. BALANCED targeted bispectral-index values 50 versus 35, a processed-EEG measure, and assessed delirium twice daily for 5 days: 47/253 versus 74/262 analyzed patients aged at least 60 years had delirium; odds ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.38–0.88), P=0.010. At 1 year, Abbreviated Mental Test Scores ≤6 occurred in 18/208 versus 41/205, P<0.001. These are screening results. Longer-term disorder requires diagnosis at 30 days–12 months, cognitive concern, domain-specific decline of 1–2 SD (mild) or >2 SD (major), and daily-function assessment; this was not established by that screening result.
milestones.set_by: BALANCED delirium substudy investigators, published Methods and statistical analysis, linked to ACTRN12612000632897. This significance threshold was applied to delirium and cognitive screening; the Nomenclature Consensus Working Group separately defines diagnosed postoperative neurocognitive disorder.
milestones.threshold_quote: a two-tailed P-value <0.05 was taken to indicate statistical significance with no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
